content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes TRIDE, a data augmentation strategy for early predicting a future disease, septic shock in this particular work. Using a BERT-like EHR language model inside the training loop to generate synthetics samples that causes the largest loss, the actual disease prediction model can achieve a better temporal robustness, which is difficult to achieve due to the increasing data scarcity as the prediction window increases. On two real-world datasets, TRIDE is compared with various baseline models, and demonstrate increased predictive performance.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: 
- The paper address an important and a practical problem, namely temporal robustness in early disease prediction, although a niche problem for ICLR audience.
- The idea of placing data augmentation within a training loop, and dynamically adjusting the degree of transformation is interesting.
- Some experiment results show an improved performance of TRIDE, and it is more meaningful as the datasets were derived from real-world healthcare systems.

Weaknesses:
- The biggest weakness is that the proposed solution (i.e. synthesize samples in a way that maximizes the loss) is probably not the optimal solution to the problem addressed (i.e. data scarcity increases as prediction window increases). The proposed solution is a general solution to any time-series-based prediction tasks with insufficient training samples, not just the early disease prediction setting. If the paper wanted to focus on the temporal robustness for early disease prediction, it should have devised a more specific solution tailored for that particular task so as to maximize temporal robustness. 
- As mentioned above, TRIDE is general enough to be used for any time-series-based prediction tasks. But the paper only demonstrates its performance on a very specific task of septic shock prediction, although important in the healthcare domain. Therefore it begs the question whether this kind of approach will generalize to other tasks that ICLR audience might be more generally interested in, such as time-series prediction.
- The choices made in the proposed method seem largely arbitrary. For example, the gradient attribution is used in the upper-level and the self-attention strength to CLS is used in the lower-level, and the value \theta is used for both selecting the number of x_i's as well as the number of to-be-masked tokens inside each x_i, all of this are largely heuristic-driven. This makes it hard to believe TRIDE will generalize well to other similar tasks beyond just early prediction of septic shock.
- Further point regarding the lacking rigor in methodolgy: Is there a guarantee that the synthesized sample will not break realism, or be out-of-distribution? For example, when a mask is applied to an essential token for predicting septic shock, and EHR-BERT replaces it with a clinically infeasible/incorrect token, this will only harm the prediction performance of the model. There should be discussion regarding this point, as to how to prevent it, or how this will not be a problem. Just claiming that the performance increased anyway is not enough.
- Also, why is it a good idea to detect the token most highly impacting the loss funciton, then replace it with some other token? Wouldn't it be better to detect the most weakly impacting token and replace it with EHR-BERT?
- Experiment results are less than impressive. Overall, TRIDE's performance is not often statistcally significant compared to timeBERT. And the comparison in Figure 4 (which is probably the most important experiment, as it directly relates to the paper's claim "TRIDE increases temporal robustness") should be between TRIDE and timeBERT, not between TRIDE and EHR (which is the worst performing model in all experiments). 
- The description of the structure of the dataset is severly insufficient. The concept of two-level data structure is suddenly introduced in Section 2.2.2, and it is hard to connect it to the data description in Section 2.1. Moreover, many terms are used without a clear definition, such as "event", "symptom" (in Fig.3) and "Norm" (in Fig.3). Also, it is hard to understand, in Section 2.1, how N can used as both the total number of patients (which makes x_1 and x_2 two different patients) or total number of hospital visits (which makes x_1 and x_2 the same patient).

Questions:
- What is the AnonymizedWork in Section 2.2?
- What is the definition of \theta^* in line 10 of Algorithm 1?
- What is the exact definition of an "event"? Is this the same thing as a "symptom"? Then what is the definition of a "symptom"? Is it a single lab measure for multiple vitals?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: Details regarding the EHR data structure is insufficient. See weakness for more details.

Quality: The experiments are reasonably conducted, but Fig.4 should be revised (see weakness)

Novelty: The paper proposes a simple and reasonable solution to an interesting problem, but the solution is mostly heuristic-driven, and it is doubtful if this will generalize to other similar tasks.

Reproducibility: The dataset is not shared, thus zero reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper proposes an intuitive data augmentation solution for increaing the temporal robustness in early disease prediction problem. Although the proposed solution seems reasonable, it is not a specific solution tailored to the addressed problem, and the experiment results are rather weak to support the claim. 
The paper could be revised to delve deeper into the addressed problem (increasing temporal robustness in early detection of disease), propose a more customized solution, and submitted to a more relevant venue (e.g. ML4H, CHIL, JAMIA, JBHI), or it could broaden the scope to tackle data sparcity problem in general time-series prediction via data augmentation.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper aims to improve clinical risk prediction performance by proposing a new data augmentation method. The authors present TRIDE, a temporal, robust, and informative data augmentation framework that can learn temporal representations of EHRs and use them to generate diverse and meaningful training samples by optimizing the level of data transformation. The experimental results on two real-world datasets show the proposed TRIDE outperforms the baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. The authors present a new data augmentation framework to generate diverse samples to improve risk prediction performance.

Weaknesses:
1. The novelty is somewhat incremental.
    a) The main contribution of the paper is the proposed data augmentation method. The idea of data augmentation (i.e., selecting the important token to mask) is similar to adversarial attack methods, which slightly modify inputs (e.g., by deleting or inserting one word) to change the model output. It would be better if the authors compared the proposed TRIDE with some data augmentation baselines with adversarial attack methods (e.g., [1-3]).
    b) The authors claimed that TRIDE is the first data augmentation approach for EHRs. However, some existing work (e.g., [4-5]) has already studied the data augmentation problem in EHRs, which are supposed to be cited and compared with the proposed model. The concept of data augmentation for EHRs is not new.

2. Some necessary related-works (e.g., data augmentation studies [4-5]) are not cited.

3. The experiments could be improved:
    a) The authors discretized the variables when predicting septic shock, which would cause information loss. The details of discretization are unclear. It would be better if the author gave references for the data preprocessing and conducted experiments to show whether the discretization (positively or negatively) affects the risk prediction performance.
    b) It would be better if the authors compared the proposed data augmentation method with more baselines, including data augmentation methods [4,5] and adversarial attack methods [1-3].
    c) The proposed model is just comparable to the baselines in MAYO dataset on AUC.
    d) It would be better if the authors conducted an ablation study to show how much the data augmentation method (which is the main contribution of the paper) improves the proposed model and the baselines. The data augmentation method could be easily combined with attention-based baselines.
    e) It is unclear how many tokens are masked in the experiments when generating synthetic samples. How does the hyper-parameter affect the model performance?
    f) How to find the best value for probability p in Algorithm 1? It would be if the author showed how the model is sensitive to the parameter.

4. The authors claimed the work is “motivated by ANONYMIZEDWORK”. What is the ANONYMIZEDWORK?

5. Both EHR data and implementation code are not available.

[1] Huangzhao Zhang, Hao Zhou, Ning Miao, and Lei Li. 2019. Generating fluent adversarial examples for natural languages. In Proceedings of the 57th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, pages 5564–5569, Florence, Italy. Association for Computational Linguistics.

[2] Moustafa Alzantot, Yash Sharma, Ahmed Elgohary, Bo-Jhang Ho, Mani Srivastava, and Kai-Wei Chang. 2018. Generating natural language adversarial examples. In Proceedings of the 2018 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, pages 2890–2896, Brussels, Belgium. Association for Computational Linguistics.

[3] Yong Xie, Dakuo Wang, Pin-Yu Chen, Jinjun Xiong, Sijia Liu, and Sanmi Koyejo, “A Word is Worth A Thousand Dollars: Adversarial Attack on Tweets Fools Stock Prediction,” Annual Conference of the North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (NAACL), 2022

[4] Kennedy G, Dras M, Gallego B. Augmentation of Electronic Medical Record Data for Deep Learning. Studies in health technology and informatics, 2022, 290: 582-586.

[5] Wanyan T, Zhang J, Ding Y, et al. Bootstrapping your own positive sample: Contrastive learning with electronic health record data. arXiv preprint arXiv:2104.02932, 2021.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose a novel method to provide temporally robust prediction for EHR data using a data augmentation technique. They validated the proposed method on a real-world dataset and provided some details around the data augmentation process
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Some of the key strengths of the paper are as follows

- The author study an important problem of clinical significance. For adverse events, improving the prediction horizon can lead to better clinical intervention measures
- The proposed data augmentation scheme is simple and the results when compared to the identified baselines show promising performance
- The authors have provide good traces of the algorithm steps that may improve the reproducibility of the method

Some ways the paper can be improved upon are as follows

- The authors identified the lack of training data for longer horizons as one of the problems. However, the paper doesn't consider the relevant clinical implications of the method. Longer horizon prediction should be accompanied by uncertainties - typically the uncertainty over prediction horizon increases over the horizon. 
- Furthermore, the samples augmented by the method may need to have clinical significance. There has been past work on learning Auto Encoders and GANs to generate data along the plausible manifold - it may be important for the authors to compare against naive extensions of existing data augmentation algorithms and discuss the possible benefits
- On a continued manner, the algorithm seems to sample more along earlier horizons. It may be important to present a deeper analysis along relevant sub-groups to ensure that the data augmentations preserves the diversity of samples both from a generalization perspective as well as as from fairness perspectives.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The method is simple and the provided algorithm traces make it better suited for reproducibility. However, the  impact of the proposed augmentation schema hasn't been established in the current form of the paper
content.summary_of_the_review: The papers presents an interesting problem and a simple solution. However, the paper in its current form, doesn't justify the novelty and the impact. Apart from the previously outlined aspects, the authors may want to improve the presentation of the paper. Especially, certain aspects such as Section 2.2 where AnonymizedWork is referred to without citation makes the paper harder to follow. The writeup may benefit from a revision to improve the clarity of the presentation

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper focuses on data augmentation for EHR data to help improve the disease early prediction task. It proposes a framework called TRIDE that generates synthetic data from sampled data pairs in the training data. It utilizes a pre-trained EHR language model to generate the synthetic data. Experiments are done to predict septic shock using real-world EHRs collected from two medical systems.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Data augmentation for EHR is indeed an important and interesting research issue to be tackled. The methods and ideas presented in this paper could be of some value. However, there are many important details missing in the current submission. Some examples are:
- Page 3: a pre-trained EHR language model $\mathcal{G}$ similar to CEHR-BERT is used but there is no further description of this pre-trained model. CEHR-BERT is a model developed for event sequences. It is unclear how to use a model similar to CEHR-BERT for multi-variate irregular time series (as described on Page 2).
- The transformation level $\theta$ is not defined.
- In Algorithm 1, line 7 maximizes a "gradient" of a function $\mathcal{L}$. It is not explained what this line means.
- Page 4: It reads, "because we utilize RNN-based models such as LSTM, ...". It is not explained what is this LSTM, is it the model used for prediction? or is it the pre-trained model? What is the detailed configuration/architecture of this LSTM?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The submission may contain some interesting ideas, but the fact that too many important technical details are not well explained, which makes the paper very difficult to follow.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, this paper aims at tackling the temporal robustness problem of disease early detection from the perspective of data augmentation, which makes a lot of sense. However, the presentation of the current version needs significant improvement to allow readers to understand the technical details of the proposed method.

content.title: TRIDE: A Temporal, Robust, and Informative Data Augmentation Framework for Disease Progression Modeling
content.abstract: Modeling the progression of a target disease using electronic health records (EHRs), especially early predicting the onset of a disease, is critical for timely and accurate clinical interventions. While numerous deep learning-based prediction models have shown great success in handling sequential multivariate data such as EHRs, they often lack temporal robustness. This is problematic because they may not perform consistently well across different early prediction hours as training data become scarce upon targeting further future. Indeed, having even one weak point of time can significantly restrict the reliability of the models. In this work, we present TRIDE, a temporal, robust and informative data augmentation framework that can learn temporal representations of EHRs and use them to generate diverse and meaningful training samples by optimizing the level of data transformation. We validate TRIDE on modeling the progression of an extremely challenging disease, septic shock, by using real-world EHRs collected from two different medical systems. Our results show that TRIDE significantly outperforms strong baseline models across different prediction times and datasets, and thus enhances the temporal robustness. Further, we provide in-depth analyses of the generated samples and estimated model parameters to clarify the processes.
